analysis.one_liner: Lets farmers save and replant seed from patented crops by paying a government-set fee instead of buying new seed.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing, a vote, or even a committee mark-up after being referred to two House committees in July 2009, and expired when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Companies that sell genetically modified seed patent it and require farmers to buy fresh seed every year and sign contracts promising not to save harvested seed for replanting. This bill would have let farmers legally save and replant that seed by registering with the Department of Agriculture and paying a fee set by the government, with the money passed on to the patent holders. It would also have voided the contract clauses that ban seed saving, and put a tariff on products made abroad from American genetically modified seed sold more cheaply overseas.
analysis.who_benefits: Farmers who plant patented seed, especially growers of genetically modified corn, soybeans, and cotton, who now buy new seed each season under contracts forbidding seed saving. Under the bill they could replant their own harvested seed after registering and paying a fee, cutting one of their largest yearly input costs.

how_it_helps.text: Farmers could retain seed harvested from patented seed for their own replanting if they notify the Secretary of Agriculture of the type and quantity and pay a fee set by the Secretary [S2] [S3].
A farmer retaining seed under the bill would not be bound by any contract clause limiting seed saving or requiring royalties and licensing fees for that seed [S3].
The bill allowed refunds or fee adjustments if a farmer could not plant or harvest the retained seed because of a natural disaster [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Seed patent holders, chiefly large agricultural biotechnology companies, would no longer collect full market-price royalties from farmers who replant saved seed; instead the government would set the fee and pass it through a Treasury fund. If foreign buyers pay lower fees for exported seed, the bill would add duties on products made from that seed when they are imported back into the United States.

drawbacks.text: Patent holders would no longer set their own prices for replanted seed; the Secretary of Agriculture would set the fee, which critics would say weakens the financial incentive to develop new seed varieties [S2] [S3].
The bill creates a new registration, fee-setting, and fund-distribution system run by the Department of Agriculture and Treasury, an administrative burden with costs of its own [S3].
The proposed tariff on products of exported genetically modified seed could raise prices on imported goods and invite trade disputes with exporting countries [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For farmers, the bill offered a direct cut in a major recurring cost: the ability to replant their own harvest instead of repurchasing seed every year. The trade-off is real: seed companies depend on annual sales to fund breeding research, and replacing negotiated prices with government-set fees would give them less control and possibly less revenue. Whether the savings to farmers would have outweighed any slowdown in seed innovation depends on fee levels the Secretary would have set, which the bill left open. The bill never advanced far enough for those questions to be tested in committee.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Agriculture and Ways and Means committees on the day it was introduced, neither committee ever acted on it, and it died when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Representative Marcy Kaptur introduced the bill in the House on July 22, 2009 [S1] [S3].
The same day, it was referred to the House Agriculture Committee and, in addition, to the House Ways and Means Committee [S5].
No further action appears in the bill's history: no hearing, no mark-up, no floor vote [S5].
The bill attracted a single cosponsor, one House Democrat [S4].
The 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, and bills not passed by both chambers die at the end of a Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Seed patent holders, chiefly the large agricultural biotechnology companies, kept the existing system in which farmers must buy new patented seed each season and sign contracts barring seed saving. Farmers gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Seed patent holders and ag-biotech companies

industries.industry: Genetically modified seed and agricultural biotech companies
industries.note: These companies patent seed and sell farmers new seed every season under contracts forbidding replanting. The bill would have voided those contract bans and replaced the companies' own pricing with a government-set fee, cutting into their core recurring revenue.
Farmers planting patented seed could replant their own harvest after registering and paying a fee, lowering a major annual input cost.
